title: Substring with Concatenation of All Words
description:
# Substring with Concatenation of All Words

You are given a string `s` and an array of strings `words`. Every string in `words` has the same length.

A valid substring starts at some index in `s`, has total length `words.length * words[0].length()`, and can be split into word-sized pieces that use every word in `words` exactly once. If a word appears multiple times in `words`, it must appear that many times in the substring.

Return the starting indices of all valid substrings. The answer may be returned in any order.

## Example 1:

**Input:** s = "barfoothefoobarman", words = ["foo","bar"]
**Output:** [0,9]
**Explanation:** "barfoo" starts at 0 and "foobar" starts at 9.

## Example 2:

**Input:** s = "wordgoodgoodgoodbestword", words = ["word","good","best","word"]
**Output:** []
**Explanation:** The word "word" is required twice, but no length-16 substring has the exact multiset of words.

## Example 3:

**Input:** s = "barfoofoobarthefoobarman", words = ["bar","foo","the"]
**Output:** [6,9,12]

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= s.length <= 10^4`
*   `1 <= words.length <= 5000`
*   `1 <= words[i].length <= 30`
*   `s` and `words[i]` consist of lowercase English letters.

tests.description: two words can appear in either order
word multiplicity matters; one required copy is missing
overlapping aligned windows can all be valid
classic duplicate-word case with four-letter tokens
repeated identical words create many overlapping starts
total word length can exceed the source string
single-character words create valid starts at adjacent offsets
an invalid token resets the aligned window before a later valid substring
a valid substring may require the same word more than once

solutions.name: Offset Sliding Window with HashMap Counts
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build the target frequency map of `words`. For each offset modulo the word length, walk through `s` in word-sized steps, maintain a window frequency map, shrink from the left when a word is overused, and record the left boundary when the window contains exactly `words.length` tokens.

## Key Insight

A valid substring can only start at one of the `wordLength` alignment classes. Within one alignment, the problem becomes a normal sliding window over tokens instead of characters.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n * w), where `w` is the word length because each token extraction costs O(w)
- Space Complexity: O(k * w), where `k` is the number of distinct words

solutions.name: Remaining Counts Window
solutions.description:
## Approach

For each alignment, keep a mutable `remaining` map initialized from the target counts. Consuming a token decreases its remaining count. If that count becomes negative, move the left boundary forward and restore counts until the window is valid again.

## Key Insight

Instead of storing how many copies the window currently has, store how many copies are still allowed. A negative count pinpoints exactly which token forced the window to shrink.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n * w)
- Space Complexity: O(k * w)

solutions.name: Compressed Word Id Window
solutions.description:
## Approach

Map each distinct required word to an integer id. Replace hash-map window counts with integer arrays, then run the same aligned sliding-window logic over word-sized tokens.

## Key Insight

The set of legal words is fixed before scanning. Compressing words to ids keeps exact duplicate counts while avoiding repeated map bookkeeping for the moving window.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n * w)
- Space Complexity: O(k), plus the storage for the word-id map

solutions.name: Precomputed Token Id Windows
solutions.description:
## Approach

Compress required words to ids, then for each alignment precompute an array of token ids for the word-sized chunks in that alignment. A token not in `words` is stored as `-1`. Run the sliding window over these integer arrays.

## Key Insight

Separating tokenization from window movement makes resets and overuse handling explicit. The window never needs to slice the same aligned token twice.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n * w)
- Space Complexity: O(n + k)
